structure.title: Characterization of the interfacial Li-ion exchange process in a ceramic-polymer composite by solid state NMR†
structure.text:
Pierre Ranque, D<sup>a</sup> Jakub Zagórski, <sup>ab</sup> Shanmukaraj Devaraj, D<sup>a</sup> Frédéric Aguesse<sup>a</sup> and Juan Miguel López del Amo\*<sup>a</sup>

Solid-state electrolytes are key for the development of high energy density and safe Li-batteries. A very strong research effort has been made for the development of ceramic-polymer composite solid electrolytes that combine the high ionic conductivity of the ceramic phase with the ease of processability of the polymeric membrane. A crucial question for the development of such composite membranes is the detection and quantification of the Li-ion exchange processes existing at the interface between the polymer and ceramic particles. Using multidimensional solid-state NMR experiments, we unequivocally demonstrate and characterize in this work the Li-ion exchange process present in a PEO:LiTFSI-LLZO composite material. The exchange process is observed between bulk Li-ion populations in both phases, and is not only restricted to the exchange processes occurring at the interface. LiOH is detected in the composite material and its role in the polymer-ceramic Li-ion exchange process is discussed. The results obtained in this work illustrate the suitability of solid-state NMR for the characterization and rational design of interfacial Li-ion exchange properties in next generation polymer-ceramic composite materials.

Received 3rd May 2021 Accepted 19th July 2021

DOI: 10.1039/d1ta03720j

structure.title: Introduction
structure.text:
The development of a novel battery technology has become one of the critical factors for the energy transition. <sup>1-5</sup> The global implementation of intermittent renewable energies and electric vehicles requires safer, cheaper, and more efficient energy storage systems. <sup>5-8</sup> Currently, Li-ion batteries (LIBs) are one of the leading technologies for energy storage but suffer from limitations regarding safety and energy-density. <sup>9,10</sup> A possible solution would be to replace unstable and flammable organic liquid electrolytes by solid ceramic or polymer materials. <sup>8,11-13</sup> Additionally, the electrochemical stability of solid electrolytes enables the implementation of Li metal anodes and high-voltage cathodes, which are essential in the development of high energy-density batteries. <sup>11,14-17</sup> Among the solid electrolyte materials under research to date, Li-ion conductive ceramics and polymers are the most promising candidates due to their

<sup>a</sup>Centro de Investigación Cooperativa de Energías Alternativas (CIC energiGUNE), Basque Research and Technology Alliance (BRTA), Parque Tecnológico de Alava, Albert Einstein 48, 01510 Vitoria-Gasteiz, Spain. E-mail: jmlopez@cicenergigune.com 
<sup>b</sup>University of the Basque Country (UPV/EHU), Barrio Sarriena, s/n, 48940 Leioa, Spain 
† Electronic supplementary information (ESI) available: X-ray diffraction of Ga-substituted LLZO (Li<sub>6.55</sub>Ga<sub>0.15</sub>La<sub>3</sub>Zr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>12</sub>). Deconvolution of the 1D <sup>7</sup>Li spectrum. <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>7</sup>Li HETCOR of the pristine LLZO powder. Estimation of the time necessary to have an efficient Li-ion mobility within the composite electrolyte via EIS. Curve fitting results of cross-peak intensities νs. mixing time from <sup>7</sup>Li-<sup>7</sup>Li EXSY (1.3 mm rotor). See DOI: 10.1039/d1ta03720j

intrinsic properties and compatibilities with Li metal anodes and cathodes. <sup>18,19</sup> However, both have advantages and disadvantages. Ceramics can have a wide electrochemical stability and a high Li-ion conductivity at room temperature, but suffer from poor mechanical properties due to their hardness and fragility. Furthermore, the poor interaction of ceramic electrolytes with electrodes generates a non-uniform current distribution at their interfaces, which promotes the propagation of Li dendrites through grain boundaries upon cycling. <sup>20,21</sup> On the other hand, polymers are easier to process and their malleability allows a better interfacial contact with the electrodes. However, their low ionic conductivity at room temperature and inability to suppress dendrite growth (as they can be easily penetrated by sharp Li dendrites due to their soft nature)<sup>21</sup> limit their battery performances.

The use of inert inorganic fillers in polymer electrolytes was proven to be efficient for suppressing the formation of dendrites and plasticizing crystalline polymers. 22,23 Ideally, composite polymers using a Li-ion conductive ceramic filler in a polymer matrix can bring together the advantages of each component increasing considerably the total ionic conductivity, while maintaining the processability of a polymer. In this context, the combination of garnet-type ceramic oxide Li<sub>7</sub>La<sub>3</sub>-Zr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (LLZO) and polymer polyethylene oxide (PEO) is under extensive research and considered as a very promising candidate. 24-36 LLZO with suitable dopants crystallizes in a cubic phase and has a high ionic conductivity at room temperature

 $(\sigma_{\rm bulk} \approx 10^{-3} \text{ S cm}^{-1})^{37}$  along with a wide voltage window, <sup>14,38</sup> although expensive to produce.<sup>8,38,39</sup> On the other hand, PEO mixed with Li salt (i.e. LiTFSI) is less expensive, but presents a low ionic conductivity at room temperature ( $\sigma \approx 10^{-6}$  to 10<sup>-8</sup> S cm<sup>-1</sup>) due to their high crystallinity at room temperature.40

Bringing together the properties of ceramics and polymers in a single polymer matrix holds the potential for obtaining flexible self-standing membranes with enhanced electrode compatibilities and dendrite growth inhibition capabilities.<sup>17</sup> However, the influence of the ceramic particles on the ionic conductivity is not significant without the addition of plasticizers ( $\sigma \approx 10^{-6}$  to  $10^{-5}$  S cm<sup>-1</sup> at room temperature). 41,42 It has been observed that Li-ion conductive ceramic materials have a high area-specific resistance with the polymer phase ( $\sim 10^4 \Omega$ cm<sup>2</sup>).30,33 The slight increase of the conductivity of the PEO:-LiTFSI-LLZO composite, compared to the pure PEO:LiTFSI electrolyte, has been explained by the amorphization of PEO by the ceramic filler where the Li-ion diffusion pathway occurs mainly through the polymer phase for ceramic-in-polymer electrolytes.33,35,43,44 The detailed understanding of the polymer-ceramic interaction at an atomic level and the activation energies of the interfacial Li-ion transport mechanism still needs to be elucidated. Knowledge about the underlying reasons for the large activation energies associated with the Liion exchange between the ceramic and polymer phase is crucial for further development of this family of materials.

Solid-state MAS NMR is a very powerful tool for the detailed characterization of Li-ion dynamics in solid electrolyte materials.45,46 Solid-state NMR is a quantitative local technique that does not require structural ordering. This technique is therefore highly adequate for the characterization of the interfacial properties of polymer-ceramic composites. 47 Solid-state NMR characterization studies based on line shape analysis, bidimensional experiments and relaxometry measurements have been used to determine the chemical environment and dynamics of Li-ions and their counter anions in composite electrolytes.33,48-50 Furthermore, the evolution of local environments, by performing 1D 6Li NMR measurements after the cycling of composite electrolytes with <sup>6</sup>Li-enriched Li metal foil in symmetric cells (i.e. after plating and stripping experiments), give information about the Li-ion conduction process.35,36,44,51,52 However, solid-state NMR experiments focused on the interfacial properties of the ceramic-polymer interphase are very rare up to now. Recently we could demonstrate<sup>33</sup> that multidimensional solid-state NMR experiments can be implemented in order to detect the Li-ion exchange between the ceramic particles and polymer matrix. This first observation was highly relevant, as it could for the first time demonstrate that this exchange is in fact possible, and a similar method was used later on by Nkosi et al., to reveal the Li exchange between LLZO and a polyester-based co-polymer.53 The natural next step in this research is the design of composite materials where the activation energy of such Li-ion exchange is low enough to have an impact on the global Li-ion conductivity of such solid elec-This research however requires a detailed trolytes.

understanding of the Li-exchange mechanism and the interfacial chemistry.

In this paper we focus on Li-ion exchanges occurring between micrometric Li<sub>6.55</sub>Ga<sub>0.15</sub>La<sub>3</sub>Zr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>12</sub> particles and the PEO: LiTFSI (20:1) polymer matrix using several solid-state NMR techniques. Special attention is paid to determine the different Li-ion exchange processes occurring between the LLZO bulk and the polymer matrix, involving the LLZO reactive surface.

nodes.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Ceramic and Polymer Electrolytes
nodes.text: <sup>18,19</sup> However, both have advantages and disadvantages. Ceramics can have a wide electrochemical stability and a high Li-ion conductivity at room temperature, but suffer from poor mechanical properties due to their hardness and fragility. Furthermore, the poor interaction of ceramic electrolytes with electrodes generates a non-uniform current distribution at their interfaces, which promotes the propagation of Li dendrites through grain boundaries upon cycling. <sup>20,21</sup> On the other hand, polymers are easier to process and their malleability allows a better interfacial contact with the electrodes. However, their low ionic conductivity at room temperature and inability to suppress dendrite growth (as they can be easily penetrated by sharp Li dendrites due to their soft nature)<sup>21</sup> limit their battery performances.

nodes.title: Composite Electrolytes: Combining Ceramics and Polymers
nodes.text: The use of inert inorganic fillers in polymer electrolytes was proven to be efficient for suppressing the formation of dendrites and plasticizing crystalline polymers. 22,23 Ideally, composite polymers using a Li-ion conductive ceramic filler in a polymer matrix can bring together the advantages of each component increasing considerably the total ionic conductivity, while maintaining the processability of a polymer. In this context, the combination of garnet-type ceramic oxide Li<sub>7</sub>La<sub>3</sub>-Zr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (LLZO) and polymer polyethylene oxide (PEO) is under extensive research and considered as a very promising candidate.

nodes.title: Challenges and Limitations in Composite Electrolytes
nodes.text: However, the influence of the ceramic particles on the ionic conductivity is not significant without the addition of plasticizers ( $\sigma \approx 10^{-6}$  to  $10^{-5}$  S cm<sup>-1</sup> at room temperature). 41,42 It has been observed that Li-ion conductive ceramic materials have a high area-specific resistance with the polymer phase ( $\sim 10^4 \Omega$ cm<sup>2</sup>).30,33 The slight increase of the conductivity of the PEO:-LiTFSI-LLZO composite, compared to the pure PEO:LiTFSI electrolyte, has been explained by the amorphization of PEO by the ceramic filler where the Li-ion diffusion pathway occurs mainly through the polymer phase for ceramic-in-polymer electrolytes.33,35,43,44 The detailed understanding of the polymer-ceramic interaction at an atomic level and the activation energies of the interfacial Li-ion transport mechanism still needs to be elucidated. Knowledge about the underlying reasons for the large activation energies associated with the Liion exchange between the ceramic and polymer phase is crucial for further development of this family of materials.

nodes.title: Solid-State NMR as a Characterization Tool
nodes.text: Solid-state MAS NMR is a very powerful tool for the detailed characterization of Li-ion dynamics in solid electrolyte materials.45,46 Solid-state NMR is a quantitative local technique that does not require structural ordering. This technique is therefore highly adequate for the characterization of the interfacial properties of polymer-ceramic composites. 47 Solid-state NMR characterization studies based on line shape analysis, bidimensional experiments and relaxometry measurements have been used to determine the chemical environment and dynamics of Li-ions and their counter anions in composite electrolytes.33,48-50 Furthermore, the evolution of local environments, by performing 1D 6Li NMR measurements after the cycling of composite electrolytes with <sup>6</sup>Li-enriched Li metal foil in symmetric cells (i.e. after plating and stripping experiments), give information about the Li-ion conduction process.35,36,44,51,52 However, solid-state NMR experiments focused on the interfacial properties of the ceramic-polymer interphase are very rare up to now.

structure.title: Preparation of the PEO:LiTFSI-LLZO composite membrane
structure.text: The composition selected for this study was 10 vol% (31 wt%) of LLZO in PEO: LiTFSI (20:1 ethylene oxide units per Li-ion). The slurry was mixed with a magnetic stirrer to avoid any degradation of the starting materials and the membranes were obtained by solvent casting. PEO  $(M_{\rm w}=5\,000\,000~{\rm g~mol^{-1}},$ Sigma Aldrich), LiTFSI (99.95%, Sigma Aldrich) and LLZO were mixed in ACN (99.8%, Sigma Aldrich) for 12 h. The resulting homogeneous slurry was cast in a PTFE evaporating dish and dried by subsequent solvent evaporation at room temperature (24 h) under a flow of dry air and under dynamic vacuum (12 h at 50 °C). The whole preparation process was carried out in an argon filled glovebox. The membrane obtained had a thickness of 55.8 μm.

structure.title: **Electrochemical measurements**
structure.text:
The ionic conductivity of the composite membrane was measured between two stainless steel blocking electrodes, in a CR2032 coin cell. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was done on a VMP3® (BioLogic Science Instruments), from 1 MHz to 1 Hz, with an alternating current amplitude of 10 mV, in the temperature range from 25 to 80 °C. Before each EIS measurement, the cell was maintained for at least 30 minutes to reach thermal equilibrium. The resulting spectra were analyzed with EC-lab software. The conductivity values at each temperature were calculated using the following equation:

$$\sigma = \frac{t}{A} \times \frac{1}{R}$$

![](_page_2_Figure_4.jpeg)

Fig. 1 Surface morphology characterization of the composite membrane PEO:LiTFSI + 10 vol% LLZO by SEM, at magnitudes of (a)  $\times$ 300 and (b)  $\times$ 5000. (c) Nyquist plots of the composite electrolyte obtained at different temperatures, in symmetric cells (CR2032) using stainless steel current collectors. (d) Arrhenius plots of the composite, obtained from the conductivity obtained by EIS.

where t is the thickness, R the resistance and A the area.

structure.title: Solid-state NMR
structure.text:
Samples were prepared by cutting the membrane into small pieces and firmly packing them in 2.5 and 1.3 mm rotors. Magic Angle Spinning Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (MAS NMR) spectroscopy was performed using a Bruker Avance III 500 spectrometer and TopSpin software. Spectra were recorded at a rotor spinning at the magic angle (MAS frequency) of 20 kHz for 2.5 mm rotors and 50 kHz for 1.3 mm rotors. The temperature of the sample spinning at 50 kHz was calculated to be at 44 °C using a KBr temperature calibration.55 All experiments were carried out at a resonating <sup>1</sup>H frequency of 500.24 MHz. <sup>7</sup>Li and <sup>1</sup>H spectra were referenced to a 0.1 mol L<sup>-1</sup> LiCl solution and <sup>6</sup>Li with a lithium-6 carbonate solution. EXSY (2D EXchange SpectroscopY) experiments were performed using a standard three-pulse sequence with mixing times specified in each experiment. The 6Li 1D single excitation experiment was recorded using 1024 scans, a 2.5 µs pulse and 40 s of recycling delay with a total experimental time of 11 h and 30 minutes. In <sup>7</sup>Li-<sup>7</sup>Li EXSY correlations, the length of the 90° pulses applied was 2.3 µs and 8 scans were used in each incrementation with a recycling delay of 10 s. Longitudinal relaxation times were

obtained using a saturation recovery experiment for  $^7\text{Li}$ .  $T_1$  values were obtained for  $^7\text{Li}$  at the LLZO and PEO phases of 4.8 s and 1.5 s respectively.  $^6\text{Li}-^6\text{Li}$  EXSY correlations were obtained using 2.5  $\mu$ s pulses and 24 scans.  $^1\text{H}$  to  $^6\text{Li}$  cross-polarization (CP) experiments were obtained using a CP mixing time of 1.9 ms and a recycling delay of 3 s.

 $^1\text{H}^{-7}\text{Li}$  2D Heteronuclear (HETCOR) experiments were performed using a  $^1\text{H}^{-7}\text{Li}$  cross polarization step of 1 ms, a recycling delay of 3 s and a proton pulse of 3.6  $\mu s$ . The  $^1\text{H}^{-6}\text{Li}$  CP spectrum was obtained using 1.9 ms mixing time, a 3.8  $\mu s$   $^1\text{H}$  pulse, and 5 s recycling delay. A pseudo 3D experiment was used by combination of a  $^1\text{H}$  to  $^6\text{Li}$  CP step with a EXSY mixing with the experimental values previously mentioned for each case.

Spectra were plotted and deconvoluted using the Dmfit software.<sup>56</sup>

nodes.title: Specific 1D and 2D Experiments and Parameters
nodes.text:
The 6Li 1D single excitation experiment was recorded using 1024 scans, a 2.5 µs pulse and 40 s of recycling delay with a total experimental time of 11 h and 30 minutes. In <sup>7</sup>Li-<sup>7</sup>Li EXSY correlations, the length of the 90° pulses applied was 2.3 µs and 8 scans were used in each incrementation with a recycling delay of 10 s. Longitudinal relaxation times were

obtained using a saturation recovery experiment for  $^7\text{Li}$ . $T_1$  values were obtained for  $^7\text{Li}$  at the LLZO and PEO phases of 4.8 s and 1.5 s respectively. $^6\text{Li}-^6\text{Li}$  EXSY correlations were obtained using 2.5  $\mu$ s pulses and 24 scans. $^1\text{H}$  to  $^6\text{Li}$  cross-polarization (CP) experiments were obtained using a CP mixing time of 1.9 ms and a recycling delay of 3 s.

 $^1\text{H}^{-7}\text{Li}$  2D Heteronuclear (HETCOR) experiments were performed using a  $^1\text{H}^{-7}\text{Li}$  cross polarization step of 1 ms, a recycling delay of 3 s and a proton pulse of 3.6  $\mu s$ . The  $^1\text{H}^{-6}\text{Li}$  CP spectrum was obtained using 1.9 ms mixing time, a 3.8  $\mu s$   $^1\text{H}$  pulse, and 5 s recycling delay. A pseudo 3D experiment was used by combination of a  $^1\text{H}$  to  $^6\text{Li}$  CP step with a EXSY mixing with the experimental values previously mentioned for each case.

structure.title: Results and discussion
structure.text:
A homogeneous dispersion of LLZO particles within the PEO matrix is achieved following our developed processing of the composite membranes. Micrometric particles of 1 to 2 microns are observed by SEM with a slight degree of ceramic clustering (Fig. 1a and b).

The electrical properties of the PEO:LiTFSI + 10 vol% LLZO composite membrane were measured by AC impedance spectroscopy (see Fig. 1c). The semicircle at high and intermediate frequencies is representative of the bulk resistivity. The line at low frequencies is due to the double-layer capacitance formed at the interface between the blocking electrode (i.e. stainless steel) and the electrolyte membrane. The fit of the bulk resistivity allows to calculate the Li-ion conductivity ( $\sigma$ , in S cm<sup>-1</sup>) using the equation described in the Experimental section. The Arrhenius plot, obtained by plotting the logarithm of the conductivity versus the inverse of the temperature, has a trend similar to what was previously reported,33 with two activation energies (see Fig. 1d). The higher activation energy seen below 50 °C is due to the partial crystallization of the polymer which diminishes the Li-ion diffusion through the membrane.

The low content of ceramic filler (10 vol%) and the lack of particle cohesion exclude the possibility of a continuous pathway of the Li-ions through the ceramic particles only. The observed conductivity must be either a result of the polymer conduction only or by a more complex combination of polymerceramic pathways.

The <sup>7</sup>Li solid-state NMR spectrum of the PEO:LiTFSI + 10 vol% LLZO composite sample is shown in Fig. 2a. Two main signals are observed in this spectrum with different chemical shifts and linewidths. The narrow line centered at -1.29 ppm is assigned to Li-ions in the PEO:LiTFSI phase in agreement with previous NMR spectra of a similar composite33 and with the corresponding spectrum of pure polymer samples.<sup>57</sup> The broader signal observed in Fig. 2a at 0.6 ppm is in good agreement with values previously reported for LLZO in the composite<sup>33</sup> and pure LLZO samples.<sup>37,54</sup> Although the presence of two main lithium components in the spectrum is clear, a proper deconvolution of the spectrum considering only two signals could not be obtained (see ESI Fig. S2†). This indicates that the presence of more than two Li-ion environments or Liion containing compounds in the sample cannot be excluded from the inspection of this spectrum only.

Our previous investigations on garnet materials by solidstate NMR revealed that LLZO is a highly hygroscopic material able to rapidly incorporate protons in the structure from moisture present in the atmosphere.37 We demonstrated that absorption of water was followed by dissociation of the proton

![](_page_3_Figure_9.jpeg)

Fig. 2 (a) <sup>7</sup>Li solid-state NMR spectrum of the PEO:LiTFSI + 10 vol% LLZO sample. Two signals centered at 0.6 and -1.29 ppm are assigned to Li populations in the LLZO and the PEO phases respectively. (b) A <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>7</sup>Li HETCOR correlation based on a CP transfer step is shown at the bottom. The dashed line is used to highlight the signal corresponding to LiTFSI in the PEO phase in both spectra. The 1D  $^{7}$ Li spectrum of the composite sample is shown at the top of the figure. (c) Schematic of the Li-ion environments detected in the composite by  ${}^{1}H-{}^{7}Li$  HETCOR.

and the hydroxyl group that further reacts with Li-ions to form LiOH at the surface of the garnet particles. These observations were later confirmed by other groups. 58-60 In order to assess the possible presence of LiOH in the composite sample, a <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>7</sup>Li 2D HETCOR NMR spectrum was recorded for the composite sample. The resulting spectrum is shown in Fig. 2b where three main signals are observed correlating distinct <sup>1</sup>H populations with nearby Li-ion reservoirs. The minor narrow signal centered at -1.3 ppm in the <sup>7</sup>Li dimension coincides with the Li signal observed for Li in the PEO phase (dashed line in the figure) and its assignment is therefore straightforward. It should be noted that the signal intensities in the 2D correlation of Fig. 2b are not quantitative, as they are based on cross-polarization (CP) correlations for transferring the magnetization and this depends directly on the strength of the <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>7</sup>Li dipolar interaction. Heteronuclear dipolar interactions are directly influenced by through-space internuclear distances and by the relative fluctuations of atoms involved. It is therefore expected that protons at the PEO phase are less effective in transferring the magnetization due to the higher natural mobility of the polymer chains compared to the fixed structures of the LLZO phases. Thus, the PEO phase will generate less intense signals in CPbased heteronuclear correlations. Additionally, the two broad signals observed in the 2D spectrum of Fig. 2b are characterized by rather similar <sup>7</sup>Li NMR chemical shifts but are clearly different in the <sup>1</sup>H dimension. The broad signal correlated with a <sup>1</sup>H chemical shift of -1.3 ppm is assigned to LiOH, in agreement with the observation made previously for a waterexposed LLZO material,37 and with the 1H signal observed for LiOH.61 This signal is intense in the 2D spectrum of Fig. 2b, but the actual amount of LiOH phase cannot be quantified from this spectrum as CP based experiments are in general nonquantitative. Finally, the <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>7</sup>Li correlated signal marked as "Li<sup>+</sup> at LLZO" in Fig. 2b is assigned to Li-ions inside the garnet structure that are in the vicinity of intercalated protons. This signal can also be observed in pure LLZO powder (see ESI Fig. S3†), which excludes the possibility that it could have originated from PEO protons coupled to <sup>7</sup>Li ions at LLZO. The three different Li-ion environments of the composite electrolyte are schematized in Fig. 2c. It should be noted that although the LiOH and the signal of Li-ions in the LLZO crystal are characterized by rather different <sup>1</sup>H chemical shifts, the difference in <sup>7</sup>Li shift is small. This is why these two phases cannot be easily differentiated in the 1D spectrum of Fig. 2a, leading to difficulties to fit the spectrum properly.

In order to increase the resolution of the Li NMR experiment, <sup>6</sup>Li NMR was conducted for this sample and the result is shown in Fig. 3a. <sup>6</sup>Li NMR spectra are generally better resolved than the corresponding <sup>7</sup>Li NMR spectra due to the lower gyromagnetic ratio of <sup>6</sup>Li and the lower dipolar broadening of this isotope. <sup>45</sup> Obviously, recording <sup>6</sup>Li NMR spectra suffers from long acquisition times due to the low natural abundance of this isotope (7.59%) and its lower gyromagnetic ratio. The <sup>6</sup>Li components of the spectrum shown in Fig. 3a are well deconvoluted into three signals, in agreement with the conclusions made in Fig. 2b.

In our previous work the interfacial Li-ion exchange process in a PEO:LiTFSI-LLZO composite was detected by a <sup>7</sup>Li 2D EXSY correlation with a mixing time of 0.6 seconds.<sup>33</sup> However, the presence of correlation signals in a <sup>7</sup>Li 2D experiment can be attributed to both the physical exchange process of Li-ion migration through the polymer–garnet interface and a spin diffusion effect based on possible dipolar interactions between nearby <sup>7</sup>Li nuclei.<sup>62</sup> We discarded this latter possibility due to the expected long internuclear distances between Li-ions at the interface between the polymer and garnet phases.

However, to unequivocally discriminate the origin of the correlation signals observed in the <sup>7</sup>Li EXSY spectrum, a <sup>6</sup>Li 2D EXSY experiment was conducted (Fig. 3a). In the case of <sup>6</sup>Li, the possibility of spin diffusion can be totally ruled out, as for this isotope the probability of observing two <sup>6</sup>Li isotopes at a close distance is negligible due to its low natural abundance. Additionally, the low dipolar moment of 6Li would make spin diffusion through dipolar interactions even more unlikely. The result of the <sup>6</sup>Li 2D EXSY spectrum reveals the presence of crosspeaks interconnecting the resonances of the <sup>6</sup>Li in the PEO and garnet phases. This result clearly demonstrates the presence of dynamic physical exchange processes of Li-ions between the two phases in the solid composite at 0.6 s of mixing time. Similar exchange processes have been demonstrated by <sup>6</sup>Li NMR EXSY experiments between Li-ion-containing inorganic electrolytes,63 but were never characterized before for a polymer-ceramic interface. By careful inspection of the positions of the off-diagonal signals, it can be observed that the resonance of the inorganic phase, correlated with the 6Li peak at PEO, is shifted to lower ppm values with respect to the center of the <sup>6</sup>Li overlapped signals of the inorganic phase. This shift is in agreement with the signal position expected for Li-ions in the garnet phases (as observed in Fig. 2b). This demonstrates that the physical exchange process corresponds to the reversible migration of the ions between PEO and bulk LLZO phases, as shown in Fig. 3b. Furthermore, the high intensity of the offdiagonal signals can only be explained by a bulk-to-bulk exchange process. A much lower cross peak intensity would be expected if only the Li-ion populations at the interface are subjected to a physical exchange. This result is very relevant, as it demonstrates that Li-ions are effectively able to diffuse from the organic to the inorganic Li-ion conducting phases and vice versa. This opens the possibility to generate polymer blends that efficiently use the combined conductivity of PEO and the ceramic materials by appropriate treatment of the chemical or physicochemical conditions at the interphase.

No exchange signals are evident between LLZO and LiOH phases in Fig. 3a, although this does not exclude the possibility of Li-ions from LiOH exchanging with both phases, or even acting as an intermediate for the exchange reaction. The <sup>6</sup>Li NMR spectrum of Fig. 3a could not be used to accurately quantify the amount of LiOH in the sample due to the strong overlapping of the signals.

In order to further explore the exchange process occurring between the three Li-containing compounds detected in the composite (PEO, LLZO and LiOH), a pseudo 3D NMR experiment was conducted. In this experiment a first  $^1\text{H}-^6\text{Li}$  CP step is

![](_page_5_Figure_5.jpeg)

Fig. 3 (a)  $^{6}$ Li 1D spectrum of the composite material. (b)  $^{6}$ Li  $^{-6}$ Li EXSY spectrum obtained with 0.6 seconds of mixing time is shown at the bottom. The 1D <sup>6</sup>Li spectrum of the composite sample is shown at the top of the figure. Dashed lines are a guide to the eye connecting the different resonances in the 1D and the 2D plots. (b) Schematic of the Li-ion exchange observed in the composite by  $^6\text{Li-}^6\text{Li}$  EXSY.

followed by an EXSY step. Different signal intensities are obtained after the first CP step due to the different internuclear distances and relative motions between <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>6</sup>Li in PEO, LLZO and LiOH. In this context, the intensity of the LiOH signal is expected to significantly increase as both the interatomic

distance and the mobility are expected to be the lowest in this phase. This is experimentally confirmed in the 1D spectrum of Fig. 4a. Adding an EXSY step after this CP experiment facilitates the detection of possible exchange processes involving the LiOH population. The result of the 2D version of this 3D experiment is

![](_page_5_Figure_9.jpeg)

Fig. 4 (a) <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>6</sup>Li CP spectrum. (b) <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>6</sup>Li CP experiment coupled to a EXSY step in a pseudo 3D NMR experiment at different mixing times (1 ms in black,  $1.2 \, \text{s}$  in green contours). (c) Schematic representing the polarization of Li-ions during the  $^1\text{H}-^6\text{Li}$  CP experiment (top) and the exchange of these Li-ions observed after the <sup>6</sup>Li-<sup>6</sup>Li EXSY step (bottom).

![](_page_6_Figure_4.jpeg)

Fig. 5 (a)  $^{7}\text{Li} - ^{7}\text{Li}$  EXSY spectrum obtained in a 1.3 mm rotor with a mixing time of 0.1 s. (b) Evolution of cross-peak intensity as a function of different mixing times (3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 120 and 200 ms) obtained from the 2D EXSY measurements at room temperature.

shown in Fig. 4b. The <sup>6</sup>Li CP spectrum of Fig. 4a is characterized by two signals corresponding to <sup>6</sup>Li from LLZO and LiOH phases. No signal was detected for the PEO phase as in this case the CP transfer step is precluded due to the combination of <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>6</sup>Li motions and the longer interatomic <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>6</sup>Li distances. The resulting 2D spectra obtained after including an EXSY step to this CP experiment are shown in Fig. 4b at two different mixing times (1 ms in black and 1.2 s in green). Exchange signals are observed connecting both LiOH and LLZO phases to the resonance corresponding to <sup>6</sup>Li in the PEO phase at around –1.3 ppm. This result demonstrates that Li-ions in the LiOH phase are also involved in a physical exchange process with the PEO phase at the mixing time of 1.2 s. In addition, cross peaks are also observed connecting the LLZO and the LiOH phases.

The results of the 2D experiments shown in Fig. 3 and 4 demonstrate that Li-ions are able to diffuse between all three lithium-containing phases of the material (PEO, LiOH and LLZO), as presented in Fig. 4c. Since the LiOH phase is formed by the reaction of residual water molecules at the surface of the garnet material, we expect this phase to be present at the interface between PEO and LLZO materials.<sup>60</sup> It still remains a challenge to elucidate if the intermediate LiOH acts as an intermediate in the reversible exchange of Li-ions between the PEO and garnet phases.

As a next step, <sup>7</sup>Li 2D EXSY experiments were performed using high speed 1.3 mm rotors in order to obtain better resolved spectra that enable the accurate quantification of the exchange process of Li-ions between PEO and LLZO phases. An example of the obtained spectra is shown in Fig. 5a. Fast MAS frequencies are used in solid-state NMR experiments in order to reduce the line broadening generated by anisotropic interactions, like the dipolar and first order quadrupolar interactions. Increasing MAS frequencies in the <sup>7</sup>Li-<sup>7</sup>Li 2D EXSY experiments is therefore beneficial for the signal resolution and by further avoiding the (unlikely) possibility of dipolar-based spin diffusion artifacts. <sup>64</sup> It should be noted that spin diffusion between nearby <sup>7</sup>Li ions can in general not be ruled out. In the present situation however, flip-flop processes are in general quite

unlikely as the Li positions that are exchanging in the process are placed in different phases (the LLZO and the PEO) and therefore presumably separated by a relatively large distance. We should additionally consider that both phases are Li-ion conductors and that the intrinsic Li-ion mobility in the system would further reduce possible dipolar interactions. The build-up of the cross-peak intensities of the 2D experiments shown in Fig. 5a as a function of different mixing times is shown in Fig. 5b. The build-up rate of the off-diagonal signals is very well fitted considering a single exponential function. The time constant of the exponential function is 35.6 ms at room temperature and the plateau for the diffusion process is observed at around 150 ms. At this time, the Li-ion populations in the different reservoirs are approximately equilibrated. An accurate determination of the activation energy for the Li-ion transport at the interface, based on the rates obtained by NMR, would require a precise quantification of the effective surface active at the interface. In order to obtain a measurable increment in the total Li-ion conductivity of the composite material originating from Li-ion diffusion pathways that combine the polymer and ceramic environments in the timescale of the EIS experiments, the equilibration of the Li-ion populations should occur at significantly shorter mixing times. From EIS measurement at room temperature, the bulk resistance is observed at frequencies above 5000 Hz (see ESI Fig. S4†). Thus, it can be possible to roughly estimate that the timescale necessary for having a proper exchange (under an electrochemical field), in order to actively participate in the bulk ionic conductivity, should be shorter than 0.2 ms. This result is in agreement with the ionic conductivity results of the PEO:-LiTFSI-LLZO system suggesting that the ionic conductivity is dominated by the polymer phase.

nodes.title: Electrical Properties and Conductivity Analysis
nodes.text: The semicircle at high and intermediate frequencies is representative of the bulk resistivity. The line at low frequencies is due to the double-layer capacitance formed at the interface between the blocking electrode (i.e. stainless steel) and the electrolyte membrane. The fit of the bulk resistivity allows to calculate the Li-ion conductivity ( $\sigma$ , in S cm<sup>-1</sup>) using the equation described in the Experimental section. The Arrhenius plot, obtained by plotting the logarithm of the conductivity versus the inverse of the temperature, has a trend similar to what was previously reported,33 with two activation energies (see Fig. 1d). The higher activation energy seen below 50 °C is due to the partial crystallization of the polymer which diminishes the Li-ion diffusion through the membrane. The low content of ceramic filler (10 vol%) and the lack of particle cohesion exclude the possibility of a continuous pathway of the Li-ions through the ceramic particles only. The observed conductivity must be either a result of the polymer conduction only or by a more complex combination of polymerceramic pathways.

nodes.title: 1D 7Li NMR Spectroscopy of the Composite
nodes.text: The <sup>7</sup>Li solid-state NMR spectrum of the PEO:LiTFSI + 10 vol% LLZO composite sample is shown in Fig. 2a. Two main signals are observed in this spectrum with different chemical shifts and linewidths. The narrow line centered at -1.29 ppm is assigned to Li-ions in the PEO:LiTFSI phase in agreement with previous NMR spectra of a similar composite33 and with the corresponding spectrum of pure polymer samples.<sup>57</sup> The broader signal observed in Fig. 2a at 0.6 ppm is in good agreement with values previously reported for LLZO in the composite<sup>33</sup> and pure LLZO samples.<sup>37,54</sup> Although the presence of two main lithium components in the spectrum is clear, a proper deconvolution of the spectrum considering only two signals could not be obtained (see ESI Fig. S2†). This indicates that the presence of more than two Li-ion environments or Liion containing compounds in the sample cannot be excluded from the inspection of this spectrum only.

nodes.title: 2D 1H-7Li HETCOR NMR for Li Environments
nodes.text: In order to assess the possible presence of LiOH in the composite sample, a <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>7</sup>Li 2D HETCOR NMR spectrum was recorded for the composite sample. The resulting spectrum is shown in Fig. 2b where three main signals are observed correlating distinct <sup>1</sup>H populations with nearby Li-ion reservoirs. The minor narrow signal centered at -1.3 ppm in the <sup>7</sup>Li dimension coincides with the Li signal observed for Li in the PEO phase (dashed line in the figure) and its assignment is therefore straightforward. It should be noted that the signal intensities in the 2D correlation of Fig. 2b are not quantitative, as they are based on cross-polarization (CP) correlations for transferring the magnetization and this depends directly on the strength of the <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>7</sup>Li dipolar interaction. Heteronuclear dipolar interactions are directly influenced by through-space internuclear distances and by the relative fluctuations of atoms involved. It is therefore expected that protons at the PEO phase are less effective in transferring the magnetization due to the higher natural mobility of the polymer chains compared to the fixed structures of the LLZO phases. Thus, the PEO phase will generate less intense signals in CPbased heteronuclear correlations. Additionally, the two broad signals observed in the 2D spectrum of Fig. 2b are characterized by rather similar <sup>7</sup>Li NMR chemical shifts but are clearly different in the <sup>1</sup>H dimension. The broad signal correlated with a <sup>1</sup>H chemical shift of -1.3 ppm is assigned to LiOH, in agreement with the observation made previously for a waterexposed LLZO material,37 and with the 1H signal observed for LiOH.61 This signal is intense in the 2D spectrum of Fig. 2b, but the actual amount of LiOH phase cannot be quantified from this spectrum as CP based experiments are in general nonquantitative. Finally, the <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>7</sup>Li correlated signal marked as "Li<sup>+</sup> at LLZO" in Fig. 2b is assigned to Li-ions inside the garnet structure that are in the vicinity of intercalated protons. This signal can also be observed in pure LLZO powder (see ESI Fig. S3†), which excludes the possibility that it could have originated from PEO protons coupled to <sup>7</sup>Li ions at LLZO. The three different Li-ion environments of the composite electrolyte are schematized in Fig. 2c. It should be noted that although the LiOH and the signal of Li-ions in the LLZO crystal are characterized by rather different <sup>1</sup>H chemical shifts, the difference in <sup>7</sup>Li shift is small. This is why these two phases cannot be easily differentiated in the 1D spectrum of Fig. 2a, leading to difficulties to fit the spectrum properly.

nodes.title: 6Li-6Li EXSY NMR for Li-ion Exchange
nodes.text: In our previous work the interfacial Li-ion exchange process in a PEO:LiTFSI-LLZO composite was detected by a <sup>7</sup>Li 2D EXSY correlation with a mixing time of 0.6 seconds.<sup>33</sup> However, the presence of correlation signals in a <sup>7</sup>Li 2D experiment can be attributed to both the physical exchange process of Li-ion migration through the polymer–garnet interface and a spin diffusion effect based on possible dipolar interactions between nearby <sup>7</sup>Li nuclei.<sup>62</sup> We discarded this latter possibility due to the expected long internuclear distances between Li-ions at the interface between the polymer and garnet phases. However, to unequivocally discriminate the origin of the correlation signals observed in the <sup>7</sup>Li EXSY spectrum, a <sup>6</sup>Li 2D EXSY experiment was conducted (Fig. 3a). In the case of <sup>6</sup>Li, the possibility of spin diffusion can be totally ruled out, as for this isotope the probability of observing two <sup>6</sup>Li isotopes at a close distance is negligible due to its low natural abundance. Additionally, the low dipolar moment of 6Li would make spin diffusion through dipolar interactions even more unlikely. The result of the <sup>6</sup>Li 2D EXSY spectrum reveals the presence of crosspeaks interconnecting the resonances of the <sup>6</sup>Li in the PEO and garnet phases. This result clearly demonstrates the presence of dynamic physical exchange processes of Li-ions between the two phases in the solid composite at 0.6 s of mixing time. Similar exchange processes have been demonstrated by <sup>6</sup>Li NMR EXSY experiments between Li-ion-containing inorganic electrolytes,63 but were never characterized before for a polymer-ceramic interface. By careful inspection of the positions of the off-diagonal signals, it can be observed that the resonance of the inorganic phase, correlated with the 6Li peak at PEO, is shifted to lower ppm values with respect to the center of the <sup>6</sup>Li overlapped signals of the inorganic phase. This shift is in agreement with the signal position expected for Li-ions in the garnet phases (as observed in Fig. 2b). This demonstrates that the physical exchange process corresponds to the reversible migration of the ions between PEO and bulk LLZO phases, as shown in Fig. 3b. Furthermore, the high intensity of the offdiagonal signals can only be explained by a bulk-to-bulk exchange process. A much lower cross peak intensity would be expected if only the Li-ion populations at the interface are subjected to a physical exchange.

nodes.title: Implications of Li-ion Exchange for Conductivity
nodes.text: This result is very relevant, as it demonstrates that Li-ions are effectively able to diffuse from the organic to the inorganic Li-ion conducting phases and vice versa. This opens the possibility to generate polymer blends that efficiently use the combined conductivity of PEO and the ceramic materials by appropriate treatment of the chemical or physicochemical conditions at the interphase. No exchange signals are evident between LLZO and LiOH phases in Fig. 3a, although this does not exclude the possibility of Li-ions from LiOH exchanging with both phases, or even acting as an intermediate for the exchange reaction. The <sup>6</sup>Li NMR spectrum of Fig. 3a could not be used to accurately quantify the amount of LiOH in the sample due to the strong overlapping of the signals.

nodes.title: Pseudo 3D NMR for Exchange Processes involving LiOH
nodes.text:
In order to further explore the exchange process occurring between the three Li-containing compounds detected in the composite (PEO, LLZO and LiOH), a pseudo 3D NMR experiment was conducted. In this experiment a first  $^1\text{H}-^6\text{Li}$  CP step is __IMG_a2245977__ Fig. 3 (a)  $^{6}$ Li 1D spectrum of the composite material. (b)  $^{6}$ Li  $^{-6}$ Li EXSY spectrum obtained with 0.6 seconds of mixing time is shown at the bottom. The 1D <sup>6</sup>Li spectrum of the composite sample is shown at the top of the figure. Dashed lines are a guide to the eye connecting the different resonances in the 1D and the 2D plots. (b) Schematic of the Li-ion exchange observed in the composite by  $^6\text{Li-}^6\text{Li}$  EXSY. followed by an EXSY step. Different signal intensities are obtained after the first CP step due to the different internuclear distances and relative motions between <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>6</sup>Li in PEO, LLZO and LiOH. In this context, the intensity of the LiOH signal is expected to significantly increase as both the interatomic

distance and the mobility are expected to be the lowest in this phase. This is experimentally confirmed in the 1D spectrum of Fig. 4a. Adding an EXSY step after this CP experiment facilitates the detection of possible exchange processes involving the LiOH population. The result of the 2D version of this 3D experiment is __IMG_9e38dd9c__ Fig. 4 (a) <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>6</sup>Li CP spectrum. (b) <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>6</sup>Li CP experiment coupled to a EXSY step in a pseudo 3D NMR experiment at different mixing times (1 ms in black,  $1.2 \, \text{s}$  in green contours). (c) Schematic representing the polarization of Li-ions during the  $^1\text{H}-^6\text{Li}$  CP experiment (top) and the exchange of these Li-ions observed after the <sup>6</sup>Li-<sup>6</sup>Li EXSY step (bottom). __IMG_7e2acd74__ Fig. 5 (a)  $^{7}\text{Li} - ^{7}\text{Li}$  EXSY spectrum obtained in a 1.3 mm rotor with a mixing time of 0.1 s. (b) Evolution of cross-peak intensity as a function of different mixing times (3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 120 and 200 ms) obtained from the 2D EXSY measurements at room temperature.

shown in Fig. 4b. The <sup>6</sup>Li CP spectrum of Fig. 4a is characterized by two signals corresponding to <sup>6</sup>Li from LLZO and LiOH phases. No signal was detected for the PEO phase as in this case the CP transfer step is precluded due to the combination of <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>6</sup>Li motions and the longer interatomic <sup>1</sup>H-<sup>6</sup>Li distances. The resulting 2D spectra obtained after including an EXSY step to this CP experiment are shown in Fig. 4b at two different mixing times (1 ms in black and 1.2 s in green). Exchange signals are observed connecting both LiOH and LLZO phases to the resonance corresponding to <sup>6</sup>Li in the PEO phase at around –1.3 ppm. This result demonstrates that Li-ions in the LiOH phase are also involved in a physical exchange process with the PEO phase at the mixing time of 1.2 s. In addition, cross peaks are also observed connecting the LLZO and the LiOH phases. The results of the 2D experiments shown in Fig. 3 and 4 demonstrate that Li-ions are able to diffuse between all three lithium-containing phases of the material (PEO, LiOH and LLZO), as presented in Fig. 4c. Since the LiOH phase is formed by the reaction of residual water molecules at the surface of the garnet material, we expect this phase to be present at the interface between PEO and LLZO materials.<sup>60</sup> It still remains a challenge to elucidate if the intermediate LiOH acts as an intermediate in the reversible exchange of Li-ions between the PEO and garnet phases.

nodes.title: 7Li-7Li EXSY for Exchange Rate Quantification
nodes.text:
As a next step, <sup>7</sup>Li 2D EXSY experiments were performed using high speed 1.3 mm rotors in order to obtain better resolved spectra that enable the accurate quantification of the exchange process of Li-ions between PEO and LLZO phases. An example of the obtained spectra is shown in Fig. 5a. Fast MAS frequencies are used in solid-state NMR experiments in order to reduce the line broadening generated by anisotropic interactions, like the dipolar and first order quadrupolar interactions. Increasing MAS frequencies in the <sup>7</sup>Li-<sup>7</sup>Li 2D EXSY experiments is therefore beneficial for the signal resolution and by further avoiding the (unlikely) possibility of dipolar-based spin diffusion artifacts. <sup>64</sup> It should be noted that spin diffusion between nearby <sup>7</sup>Li ions can in general not be ruled out. In the present situation however, flip-flop processes are in general quite

unlikely as the Li positions that are exchanging in the process are placed in different phases (the LLZO and the PEO) and therefore presumably separated by a relatively large distance. We should additionally consider that both phases are Li-ion conductors and that the intrinsic Li-ion mobility in the system would further reduce possible dipolar interactions. The build-up of the cross-peak intensities of the 2D experiments shown in Fig. 5a as a function of different mixing times is shown in Fig. 5b. The build-up rate of the off-diagonal signals is very well fitted considering a single exponential function. The time constant of the exponential function is 35.6 ms at room temperature and the plateau for the diffusion process is observed at around 150 ms. At this time, the Li-ion populations in the different reservoirs are approximately equilibrated. An accurate determination of the activation energy for the Li-ion transport at the interface, based on the rates obtained by NMR, would require a precise quantification of the effective surface active at the interface. In order to obtain a measurable increment in the total Li-ion conductivity of the composite material originating from Li-ion diffusion pathways that combine the polymer and ceramic environments in the timescale of the EIS experiments, the equilibration of the Li-ion populations should occur at significantly shorter mixing times.

structure.title: Conclusion
structure.text:
In this paper, the Li-ion exchange processes existing between PEO:LiTFSI and LLZO particles were elucidated by solid-state MAS NMR using a PEO:LiTFSI + 10 vol% LLZO composite

electrolyte. We confirm the spontaneous exchange process of Liions between the organic and the inorganic Li-ion conducting materials. The large intensity of the off-diagonal signals confirms that this exchange process links Li-ion populations from the bulk reservoirs in both phases, showing that this exchange mechanism is not only restricted to the polymerceramic interface. Moreover, the exchange time between Li-ion populations from the LLZO bulk and the polymer matrix follows a single exponential function with a time constant of 35.6 ms at room temperature in agreement with a homogeneous interfacial diffusion mechanism. The time measured for spontaneous Li-ion distribution among the inorganic and organic phases of around 150 ms, reveals the presence of a relatively high interfacial activation energy that precludes effective complex ceramic-polymer pathways for the Li-ion conductivity in the timescale of the conductivity measurements. Furthermore, we could detect and demonstrate that the protonated surface of the LLZO (i.e. LiOH phase) exchanges Li-ions with the LLZO bulk and the polymer matrix as well. The role of this exchange process in the observed diffusion of Li-ions between the bulk LLZO and polymer phases still needs to be clarified, as LiOH might be a required intermediate for the interfacial Li-ion exchange process. In order to clarify this point, measurements in a non-protonated LLZO surface could be required. Unfortunately, we were so far unable to synthesize samples completely free from interfacial LiOH. We could also detect in this work the presence of protons coexisting with Li-ions inside the garnet phase. These protons might additionally impact the Li-ion diffusivity in both the bulk of the garnet and the polymergarnet interface.

In general, the presented results demonstrate the potential application of organic-inorganic composite materials in all solid-state batteries, with improved conductivities and mechanical properties as we can conclude that Li-ion diffusion pathways linking the organic and the inorganic phases are in principle possible. We also highlight the importance of solidstate NMR for studying mechanisms of interfacial Li-ion exchange in composite electrolytes and in the detection of minor secondary and Li-ion conducting phases at the interface. The NMR techniques performed unveil new methods to access crucial information about ionic transport in composite electrolytes, which will enable the rational design of a compatible polymer-ceramic interface for next generation solid-state batteries.

nodes.title: General Conclusion and Future Outlook
nodes.text: In general, the presented results demonstrate the potential application of organic-inorganic composite materials in all solid-state batteries, with improved conductivities and mechanical properties as we can conclude that Li-ion diffusion pathways linking the organic and the inorganic phases are in principle possible. We also highlight the importance of solidstate NMR for studying mechanisms of interfacial Li-ion exchange in composite electrolytes and in the detection of minor secondary and Li-ion conducting phases at the interface. The NMR techniques performed unveil new methods to access crucial information about ionic transport in composite electrolytes, which will enable the rational design of a compatible polymer-ceramic interface for next generation solid-state batteries.
